latin.71: Hic D. G. insignem Calvini locum jam a nobis laudatum pag. 20. contra se citat. Quod unius delicto periisse nos tradit, sic accipe, quia ex ipso in nos corruptio transfusa sit. Neque enim sic perimus eius culpa, quasi extra culpam ipsi simus; Sed quia eius peccatum peccati nostri causa est, exitium nostrum illi Paulus adscribit. Non potuit apertius significare, peccatum Adami causam esse exitii nostri non proximam sed remotam, non immediatam, sed mediatam. Causa enim causae est causa etiam effectus, sed remota duntaxat.
latin.72: Conatur tamen tam claro loco tenebras offundere D. G. Quibus verbis, inquit, non negatur nos Adami ipsius actuali peccato perire, nec hoc etiam negat, aut negavit unquam Placeus: Sed significatur, non esse illud Adami peccatum a nostra corruptione separandum, quippe cum ex utroque confurgat idem reatus. An id verbis illis significetur, eaque ratio afferatur, iudicium esto penes Lectorem. Illud mihi satis est,
latin.73: ideo exitium nostrum Adami peccato adscribi, quia est causa peccati nostri, non dicit, quia nobis imputatur, aut quia imputatione nostrum est: sed illud distinguit a peccato nostro tanquam causam ab effectu. Est igitur a peccato Adami peccatum nostrum, & ab hoc exitium nostrum. Ita ex utroque confurgit idem reatus, ex peccato nostro proxime, ex peccato Adami remote.
latin.74: Exponit mentem suam alibi Calvinus, Peccatum originale, inquit, est naturae nostrae pravitas ac corruptio, quae primum reos facit nos irae Dei, tum etiam opera in nobis profert quae Scriptura vocat opera carnis. Sequitur ergo reatus corruptionem ut effectus causam, & quidem causam, ut loquuntur, adaequatam: subiungit enim continuo. Haec itaque duo distincte observanda: nempe quod sic omnibus naturae nostrae partibus vitiati perversique, iam ob talem duntaxat corruptionem damnati merito convictique coram Deo tenemur. Quae eadem verba, adeo tanto viro placebant, bis extant in ejus institutione, semel lib. 2. cap. 1. §. 8. & iterum lib. 4. cap. 15. §. 10.
latin.75: Addit quoque in priore loco uberioris explicationis gratia haec verba. Neque ista est alieni delicti obligatio: quod enim dicitur, nos per Adae peccatum obnoxios esse factos Dei judicio: non ita est accipiendum, ac si insones ipsi & immerentes culpam delicti ejus sustineremus: sed quia per eius transgressionem maledictione induti sumus omnes, dicitur ille nos obstrinxisse. Ab illo tamen non sola in nos poena grassata est, sed instillata ab ipso lues in nobis residet cui iure poena debetur. Quare Augustinus utcunque alienum peccatum saepe vocet (quo clarius ostendat propagine in nos derivari) simul tamen & proprium unicuique asserit. Et Apostolus ipse disertissime testatur, ideo mortem in omnes pervagatam, quod omnes peccarint, id est, involuti sint originali peccato, & eius maculis inquinati. Atque adeo infantes quoque ipsi, dum suam secum damnationem a matris utero afferunt, non alieno, sed suo ipsorum vitio sunt obstricti. Reatus igitur & damnatio & mors sequuntur corruptionem haereditariam ut effectus causam, & ob eam duntaxat non autem ob peccatum actuale Adami (nisi remote & mediate) morti sumus addicti.

pass_a.71: At this point Garissoles cites against himself a famous Calvin passage that we already praised at page 20. The teaching that we died through one man's offense should be taken thus: corruption was transmitted from him into us. We do not die under his fault as people who ourselves stand outside fault. Rather, because his sin causes our sin, Paul credits our destruction to him. Nothing could show more plainly that Adam's sin is our ruin's cause as remote, not proximate; as mediate, not immediate. A cause of a cause is still a cause of the effect, but only a remote cause.
pass_a.72: Even so, Garissoles tries to throw darkness on a passage that is so clear. He says those words do not deny that we die by Adam's own actual sin — and Placeus does not deny that either, and never has. What the words mark, he says, is that Adam's sin must not be cut off from our corruption, because the same guilt rises from both. Whether the words mean that, and whether that is the reason given, the Reader may judge. For me this is enough:
pass_a.73: namely that our destruction is credited to Adam's sin because that sin causes our sin. Calvin does not say it is because the sin is imputed to us, or because imputation makes it ours. He sets that sin apart from our sin the way a cause is set apart from its effect. So our sin comes from Adam's sin, and our destruction comes from our sin. Thus the same guilt rises from both: from our sin as the near cause, from Adam's sin as the far cause.
pass_a.74: Calvin states his mind elsewhere. Original sin, he says, is our nature's wickedness and corruption. First it makes us liable to God's anger; then it also produces in us the works Scripture names works of the flesh. So guilt follows corruption as an effect follows its cause — and follows it as what they call an adequate cause. He adds at once: two points must be kept distinct — we are ruined and twisted in every part of our nature, and for that corruption alone we already stand rightly condemned and convicted before God. Those same words pleased him so much that they appear twice in the Institutes: book 2, chapter 1, section 8, and book 4, chapter 15, section 10.
pass_a.75: In the earlier place he also adds these words for a fuller explanation. This is not liability for another man's crime. When it is said that Adam's sin made us liable to God's judgment, do not hear it as if we, guiltless and undeserving, were carrying the blame of his crime. Rather, because his trespass clothed us all with the curse, he is said to have bound us. Yet penalty alone did not rush from him upon us: a contagion poured from him still lives in us, and penalty is owed to it by right. So Augustine may often call the sin another's, in order to show more clearly that it reaches us by descent; yet he also affirms it as each person's own. And the Apostle himself testifies most expressly that death spread through all because all sinned — that is, because they were wrapped in original sin and stained by its marks. Even infants, bringing their own damnation with them from the womb, are bound by their own vice, not by another's. Therefore guilt, condemnation, and death follow hereditary corruption as effect follows cause; and for that corruption alone — not for Adam's actual sin except as a remote and mediate cause — we are bound over to death.

71: Here D. Garissoles turns against himself a distinguished place of Calvin that we already praised at page 20. "What he hands down — that we perished by the offense of one — take thus: because from him corruption was poured across into us. For we do not so perish by his fault as if we ourselves were outside fault; but because his sin is the cause of our sin, Paul ascribes our ruin to him" (Romans 5:15). He could not have marked more openly that Adam's sin is the cause of our ruin not proximate but remote, not immediate but mediate. For the cause of a cause is also a cause of the effect, yet only remote.
72: Yet D. Garissoles tries to cast darkness over a place so clear. "By which words," he says, "it is not denied that we perish by Adam's own actual sin" — and Placeus neither denies this nor has ever denied it — "but it is signified that that sin of Adam is not to be parted from our corruption, seeing that from both the same guilt rises together." Whether those words signify that, and whether that reason is brought, let judgment rest with the Reader. This is enough for me:
73: that our ruin is ascribed to Adam's sin because it is the cause of our sin. He does not say, because it is imputed to us, or because it is ours by imputation; but he distinguishes that from our sin as cause from effect. Therefore our sin is from Adam's sin, and from this our ruin. So from both the same guilt rises — from our sin proximately, from Adam's sin remotely.
74: Elsewhere Calvin unfolds his mind. "Original sin," he says, "is the depravity and corruption of our nature, which first makes us guilty of the wrath of God, then also brings forth in us works which Scripture calls works of the flesh" (Galatians 5:19). Therefore guilt follows corruption as effect follows cause — and indeed, as they say, an adequate cause: for he subjoins at once. "These two things, then, are to be observed distinctly: namely that, being thus spoiled and perverted in all the parts of our nature, we are already held before God justly damned and convicted on account of that corruption alone." Which same words so pleased so great a man that they stand twice in his Institutes — once in book 2, chapter 1, section 8, and again in book 4, chapter 15, section 10.
75: He also adds in the earlier place, for fuller explanation, these words. "Nor is this an obligation of another's offense: for what is said — that by Adam's sin we have been made liable to God's judgment — is not to be taken as if we ourselves, innocent and undeserving, were bearing the blame of his offense; but because through his transgression we have all been clothed with the curse, he is said to have bound us. Yet from him not penalty alone has rushed upon us, but a plague poured in from him resides in us, to which penalty is due by right. Wherefore Augustine, however often he may call it another's sin (so that he may show more clearly that it is derived into us by propagation), yet at the same time asserts it also as each one's own. And the Apostle himself most expressly testifies that death has wandered through unto all for this reason, that all have sinned — that is, that they have been wrapped in original sin and stained with its spots" (Romans 5:12). And so even infants themselves, while they bring with them their damnation from the mother's womb, are bound not by another's vice but by their own. Therefore guilt and condemnation and death follow hereditary corruption as effect follows cause, and on account of that alone — not, however, on account of Adam's actual sin (except remotely and mediately) — we are sentenced to death.
